title: Which Stormwater Plan Deserves a Closer Look?
audience: Environmental, civil, stormwater, and water-resources engineers, students, and curious newcomers. No prior knowledge of SWMM, green infrastructure, optimization, or machine learning is assumed.
question: When a neighborhood has many possible ways to slow stormwater and limited money for field investigation, how can an engineer find a useful shortlist without hiding a worsened storm response?
takeaway: Drainage software calculates what each declared plan does in the model. Search can choose which plan to test next. Evidence preserves how each result was made. The engineer decides what deserves real-world investigation.
source_boundary: Cedar Trace is a self-authored synthetic teaching fixture. Displayed hydraulic values come from the pinned exact-run manifest. Any cloud synchronization or provider-backed assistant workflow requires a W&B binding whose exact Restricted policy status is verified; local evidence remains authoritative. This source-build recording stays local-only and performs no upload or provider-backed call because that scope cannot be proven. It also does not demonstrate an adaptive-ML advantage, calibrated model, native release installer, or regulatory workflow.

segments.narration: Imagine you are responsible for a neighborhood where hard rain can overwhelm the drains. You have 220 improvement plans and no budget to build them all. So you draw a map: cost along the bottom, and how much less water reaches the outlet along the side. One plan looks like a bargain. It costs about 55 thousand dollars and sends a little less water out. But the picture has hidden something. In the long storm, the highest flow rate rises from 3.14 to 3.21 cubic feet per second. A second storm rises too. And the plan still misses our 6 percent reduction target. The plot did not lie. It answered a smaller question. A good decision must ask the rest.

segments.narration: This is what GI Scenario Studio is for: comparing ways to change how much runoff reaches a drainage system, and how quickly it arrives. Engineers call these features green infrastructure—rain gardens, porous pavement, planted basins, and rain barrels. If you already have a drainage model, you can open it here. For this walkthrough, we will use Cedar Trace, a tiny fictional neighborhood built for teaching. It is not a real town or a design recommendation. It gives us something safer: a complete example we can take apart. The demo stays on this computer; cloud sharing is off. Our question is simple: which plan, if any, deserves the cost of a real field investigation?

segments.narration: Before we use any software, follow the water. Rain lands on an area that drains to the same place—engineers call that area a catchment. Some water soaks into soil. Some waits in a shallow basin or rain garden. The rest runs across the surface and into pipes. Eventually it reaches an outfall, simply the point where water leaves the drainage model. The flow there rises and falls during a storm. The total area under this curve is event volume: all the water that passed. The highest point is peak flow: the highest modeled flow rate during the storm. A project can lower one without lowering the other. A different rain pattern can change both. That is why one plan must face more than one storm. These drawings are conceptual, not measured.

segments.narration: Now we can introduce SWMM, the EPA's Storm Water Management Model. Think of it as a calculator for a simplified drainage world. The engineer supplies a map of the land, junctions, pipes, and outlet; a rain pattern; and the green-infrastructure plan to test. SWMM follows those declared rules and produces modeled flows and water levels. The app reads the output, checks that the run completed and its numerical balance stayed within the declared limit, and gives each file a digital fingerprint for later. But a careful calculation is still only as good as the world described to it. SWMM cannot see a missing pipe, test the soil, or tell us whether the chosen storm represents reality. Exact calculation is not the same as field truth.

segments.narration: Before looking at answers, we write down what good enough means. This matters: if we invent the rules after seeing a favorite, the analysis becomes a story we tell ourselves. Our fictional engineer sets four rules. First, across four practice storms, at least 6 percent less water must reach the model's outlet than in the unchanged model. That unchanged model is our baseline. Second, the 30-year screening cost must stay at or below 200 thousand dollars. Third, no storm is allowed to create a higher peak flow at the outlet. A good total cannot excuse one sharper surge. Fourth, every simulation used in the decision must pass basic numerical checks. The storms and costs are invented for this lesson. And verified replay means the saved files still match the recorded runs. It does not mean the model matches a real neighborhood. With the question and rules fixed, we can look at evidence without moving the goalposts.

segments.narration: Picture four lights wired together. Under this teaching brief, a plan advances only when all four are green: enough volume reduction, acceptable cost, no peak increase, and clean runs. ALT-207 turns on all four: more than 6 percent reduction, under 200 thousand dollars, no higher peak, and four clean runs. ALT-017 is cheaper, but two lights stay red. It misses the volume target and raises two storm peaks. We do not average red lights into green ones. One required failure stops the plan.

segments.narration: Rainfall is not just a depth; timing matters. An inch falling gradually can interact with storage very differently from two inches arriving mostly at the beginning. Cedar Trace uses four artificial rain patterns so we can see that difference. One inch over one hour. Two inches over one hour, weighted toward the front. Two and a half inches spread over four hours. And a four-inch, two-hour stress test. These are not historical storms or official design events. They are practice questions. Everything else in the model stays the same while the rain changes, so the comparison is fair inside this example. One surprising lesson will come from the long, four-hour event: it creates ALT-017's worst increase at the outlet even though another storm has a much larger overall peak. The biggest storm is not automatically the one that controls every decision.

segments.narration: Now take one plan and run it through all four rain patterns. We get four answers, not one. For total volume, adding the four storm totals is useful because our teaching rule asks about their combined reduction. For peak flow, adding or averaging would destroy the question we care about: did any single storm get worse? So each peak keeps its own before-and-after comparison. ALT-017 lowers two peaks, but raises two. The long storm is worst, up 0.07 cubic feet per second. If we squash everything into one score, that red warning can disappear. Every summary is a choice about what to forget.

segments.narration: Now we decide what the software is allowed to change. Not pipe sizes. Not soil properties. Not the design of a rain garden. Only four whole-number counts of additional units at four teaching locations: planted bioretention, areas of permeable pavement, rain gardens, and groups of rain barrels. Each location has a maximum count and a stated drainage destination. The map is a diagram, not surveyed geometry. The engineering details of each practice stay fixed. The search can ask, for example, what happens after adding zero bioretention units, three pavement units, two rain-garden units, and six barrel groups to the unchanged model? It cannot invent a new soil mix or pretend a utility conflict does not exist. Automation is useful when it explores choices an engineer has deliberately admitted. Here, demo approved means allowed into the lesson—not feasible, constructible, or approved for a real site.

segments.narration: Those four additional-unit counts work like four dials. The first has five settings, the second four, the third five, and the fourth seven. Multiply them and we get 700 possible combinations, including the unchanged baseline. Testing every combination under four storms would require 2,800 SWMM runs. That complete study exists as a benchmark. The guided story is smaller: 220 chosen combinations, four storms each, plus four baseline runs—884 runs in all. It is not every possibility, and it is not a demonstration that machine learning found a better answer. Imagine the untested combinations as face-down cards. A search method may choose which card to turn over next. That choice is a question, not an answer. Only a direct SWMM run can reveal the modeled hydraulics. Search decides where to look. SWMM supplies what we see.

segments.narration: The four plain-language rules now become checks the computer can apply consistently. Water volume is measured at the same outlet and compared with the same unchanged model. Peak flow is checked separately for every storm. The teaching cost rolls installation, future upkeep, and replacement over 30 years into one today-dollar screening estimate. It keeps the lesson consistent; it is not a contractor's price or a local budget. Every option also needs four completed SWMM runs and clean numerical checks. If this tiny model reports zero for a flooding measure, that remains a modeled result—not a promise that a real street stays dry. The point of this screen is not to add more numbers. It is to stop the meaning of success from changing after an attractive plan appears.

segments.narration: This screen is showing receipts, not pretending to run a simulation. The 884 jobs were completed earlier and stored in a manifest—a list of what ran and which files belong to each result. It names the fixed SWMM version, the 220 plans, the four storms, and the numerical check for every job. The plans were ordered in a repeatable way chosen in advance; machine learning did not select this guided set. A local rerun would be different: the app would launch SWMM again, show real progress, and compare the new answers with the stored ones. That control appears only when the expected engine is actually available. It is not available in this recording, so the app does not fake it. Replay lets us inspect what happened. Rerun lets us test whether it happens again. Neither should be confused with work currently running.

segments.narration: Why did ALT-017 look so good at the beginning? Because a flat plot is a shadow. Here, better means farther left for lower cost and higher for more volume reduction. Along the visible edge, no other tested plan is at least as cheap and at least as effective while improving one of those measures. Engineers call a point like that nondominated, and the edge a Pareto frontier. The names sound like verdicts. They only describe this two-number picture. Bring back the 6 percent target and ALT-017 falls short. Bring back each storm's peak and two red increases appear. Then remember that the model's real-world fitness is still unknown. A Pareto frontier is a useful map of one tradeoff. It is not the border between acceptable and unacceptable.

segments.narration: Take one red number: plus 0.07 cubic feet per second. Imagine handing it to another engineer. Their first question should be, compared with what? The answer is the long storm: 3.14 in the unchanged model, 3.21 in ALT-017. Then comes the receipt. This plan added one rain-garden unit and six rain-barrel units. The project stores that compactly as zero, zero, one, six. It wrote the change into an input file, ran the fixed SWMM version, kept the report and detailed output, identified the files with digital fingerprints, and recorded the numerical check. That chain is called provenance: a path from a claim back to what created it. It shows how the number was made. It does not prove the model matches the real world.

segments.narration: The final product is not a winning dot. It is a handoff another engineer can question. The package carries the original question, the rules, the plans compared, the results, the model runs behind them, and the limitations that still matter. The app checks those pieces before enabling the learning export, then records which cases include complete input, report, and detailed output files. For this recording, we download a compact local summary. W&B can mirror the evidence for private collaboration only after the destination's access policy is verified. It is not verified here, so nothing uploads. The local receipt remains available. A good export does not make the conclusion larger. It makes the work easier for the next person to inspect.

segments.narration: The product's value is not an automatic winner. It is the ability to say: here are the plans, the rules we chose first, the reason each example passed or failed, and the model runs behind those statements. A practitioner can repeat this with an existing SWMM project, locally appropriate storm definitions, engineer-predefined locations, and local costs. The result will still depend on that model and its assumptions. But it is no longer a mysterious dot. It is a claim another engineer can open, question, and trace. That is the difference between trust this result and here is how to check it.
